abstract.p: In this phase 2 trial (NCT04744649), 17 patients with locally advanced Epstein-Barr virus-associated gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (cT2-4aN1-3M0) received four cycles neoadjuvant toripalimab plus capecitabine/oxaliplatin. The primary endpoint was major pathological response; secondary endpoints included pathological complete response, R0 resection, adverse events, event-free survival, overall survival, and tumor microenvironment. Paired pre-/post-treatment tissues were assessed by immunofluorescence. 16 patients underwent curative resection; 1 declined surgery. Major pathological response, pathological complete response, and ypN0 were 37.5% (6/16, 95% CI 0.15–0.65), 25.0% (4/16, 95% CI 0.07–0.52), and 81.3% (13/16, 95% CI 0.54–0.96), respectively. Major pathological response was more frequent in patients with programmed death ligand 1 ≥20 (57.1%, 95%CI 0.18-0.90). Major pathological response was associated with higher pretreatment CD8⁺ T-cell density. 35.3% reported grade 3-4 adverse events. These findings suggest that neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy demonstrated favorable efficacy with a manageable safety profile in Epstein-Barr virus-associated gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) associated gastric cancer shows uncertain immunochemotherapy benefits. This phase II clinical trial reports efficacy and safety outcomes of neoadjuvant toripalimab plus CapeOX chemotherapy regimen in locally advanced EBV-associated gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)-based combination therapies have significantly improved survival outcomes in patients with advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (GC/GEJC), and have become the new standard of care in the first-line setting1–3. In the locally advanced GC/GEJC, the role of perioperative immunochemotherapy is under active investigation, with reported pathological complete response (pCR) rates ranging from 12.9% to 22.2%4–7, and emerging evidence suggesting a potential benefit in event-free survival8. However, GC/GEJC is a biologically heterogeneous disease, and the response to perioperative immunotherapy may vary across molecular subtypes. For example, in microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) locally advanced GC/GEJC, neoadjuvant bispecific antibody therapy has achieved pCR (post-neoadjuvant therapy pathological T0N0, ypT0N0) rates of 58.6% (17/29) and 60.0% (9/15)9,10, whereas in HER2-positive tumors, perioperative regimens incorporating chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy have yielded pCR rates of 38.1% (8/21)11.

Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), also known as human herpesvirus 4 (HHV-4), is the first human oncogenic virus identified and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of several malignancies12, including EBV-associated GC/GEJC (EBVaGC), a distinct subtype that accounts for approximately 4.4% to 10% of GC/GEJC and was first defined in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) classification system13–15. EBVaGC is characterized by prominent lymphocytic infiltration16 and frequent amplification of programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) / programmed death ligand 2 (PD-L2) loci17,18, suggesting a potentially high sensitivity to ICIs. However, clinical evidence supporting the benefit of ICIs in EBVaGC remains limited, largely due to the low prevalence of EBVaGC and the lack of routine preoperative molecular classification in previous studies. Early clinical data reported an objective response rate (ORR) of 100% (6/6) with ICI monotherapy in patients with advanced EBVaGC19. However, subsequent studies have not consistently replicated this positive result: four prospective trials reported ORRs of 0% (0/6)20, 25.0% (1/4)21,22, and 33.3% (3/9)23; two retrospective studies showed ORRs of 28.5% (2/7)24 and 33.3% (2/6)25. In the large randomized trials, exploratory analyses provide further context. In the first-line CheckMate 649 trial, EBVaGC patients showed a trend toward improved survival with nivolumab plus chemotherapy (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.26–1.45) or nivolumab plus ipilimumab (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.22–2.64) compared to chemotherapy alone, although these results were not statistically significant due to the small subgroup size26. In contrast, an analysis of the second-line KEYNOTE-061 trial found that the ORR to pembrolizumab in EBVaGC patients was 13% (2/15), which was not superior to the 15% (2/13) observed with paclitaxel chemotherapy27. The reliability and consistency of EBV infection status as a predictive biomarker for response to ICIs remain inconclusive. Most of the existing evidence is based on advanced-stage patients and is limited by heterogeneity in baseline characteristics and a reliance on radiographic response assessments, which may not accurately reflect true pathological regression.

To address this gap, we conducted a prospective trial in patients with locally advanced EBVaGC to evaluate the efficacy and safety of perioperative toripalimab plus capecitabine and oxaliplatin (CapeOX). Therapeutic efficacy was assessed through the major pathological response (MPR) rate to enable a more objective evaluation of treatment response and to provide an efficient surrogate endpoint that is better suited for the rapid development of therapeutic strategies. Here, we show that toripalimab combined with CapeOX as neoadjuvant therapy for EBVaGC demonstrated a favorable MPR rate and a manageable safety profile.

sec.title: Patient characteristics and neoadjuvant therapy
sec.p:
Between May 12, 2021 and September 27, 2023, 21 patients with EBV-positive GC/GEJC were screened across three participating centers (Fig. 1). Four patients were excluded due to peritoneal metastasis (P1, n = 2) or positive peritoneal cytology (P0CY1, n = 2) based on diagnostic laparoscopy and peritoneal lavage cytology. The remaining 17 patients received the planned perioperative intervention and were included in the final analysis. Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1.Fig. 1Flow chart.

The median age of the cohort was 59.4 years (range, 40–77 years), with 94.1% (16/17) being male. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) was 0 in 88.2% (15/17). Most patients had gastric cancer (82.4%, 14/17), and 17.6% (3/17) had gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. Clinical staging included cT2N1 (n = 1), cT3N1-3 (n = 5), and cT4aN1-3 (n = 11). All patients had proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) status. PD-L1 CPS ≥ 5 was observed in 58.8% (10/17). All 17 patients (100%) completed the planned four cycles of neoadjuvant therapy. Two patients required dose reductions of capecitabine and oxaliplatin due to myelosuppression.

sec.title: Surgery and pathological outcomes
sec.p:
One patient (patient 1) declined surgery after achieving cCR. The remaining 16 patients underwent curative resection: 9 (56.3%) underwent total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy, and 7 (43.8%) underwent distal gastrectomy with D2 dissection. Fourteen of the 16 surgical patients (87.5%) underwent surgery without postponement. The surgeries for the remaining three patients were postponed for 0.2 and 2.0 months, respectively; all subsequent surgeries were successful and achieved R0 resection. Details of surgical procedures, reconstruction, lymph node dissection, and intraoperative blood loss are shown in Table 2. All surgeries were performed laparoscopically, and negative peritoneal cytology was reconfirmed intraoperatively.Table 2

Pathological response is shown in Fig. 2A. The MPR rate was 37.5% (6/16, 95%CI: 0.15–0.65). Four patients (25.0%, 4/16, 95%CI: 0.07–0.52) achieved pCR (ypT0N0). The R0 resection rate was 100% (95%CI: 0.79–1.00). Postoperative pathological staging revealed substantial tumor downstaging: 81.3% (13/16, 95%CI: 0.54–0.96) of patients achieved ypN0 status, and 62.5% (10/16, 95%CI: 0.35–0.85) had minimal invasive residual disease (ypT0-2). The distribution of ypT stages was as follows: ypT0 in 31.3% (5/16, 95%CI: 0.11–0.59), ypT1 in 12.5% (2/16), ypT2 in 18.8% (3/16), ypT3 in 25.0% (4/16), and ypT4a in 12.5% (2/16) (Source data 1, source data are provided as a Source Data file). sec.title: Postoperative therapy
sec.p: Of the 16 patients who underwent surgery, 15 (93.8%) received postoperative toripalimab plus CapeOX. Ten (62.5%) completed all four cycles, one (6.3%) completed three cycles, and four (25.0%) completed one cycle. One patient (patient 6) was unable to initiate adjuvant therapy due to anastomotic leakage. The median interval from surgery to adjuvant therapy initiation was 1.3 months (range, 0.9–2.3 months). As of July 1, 2024, all patients had completed adjuvant therapy.

sec.title: Adverse events
sec.p:
No grade 5 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were observed (Table 3). TRAEs of any grade occurred in 94.1% (16/17) of patients. Grade 3–4 TRAEs occurred in 6 patients (35.3%). Postoperative complications were evaluated using the Clavien-Dindo classification (Supplementary Table S1). Of the 16 surgical patients, 11 (68.8%) experienced at least one postoperative complication. One patient (patient 6) developed grade 3 complications, including pleural effusion, atelectasis, and anastomotic leakage, all of which resolved with conservative management.Table 3

sec.title: Survival outcomes
sec.p: As of January 31, 2025, the median follow-up was 29.8 months (95% CI: 26.2 months-41.8 months). Two patients (patients 1 and 3) experienced recurrence, and one (patient 1) died. Patient 1, who declined surgery after achieving cCR, relapsed at 16.6 months, responded to first-line immunochemotherapy, and achieved an OS of 31.8 months. Patient 3, who achieved ypT0N1M0 after surgery and completed four cycles of adjuvant therapy, experienced disease recurrence at 32.3 months. As of the data cutoff (44.8 months from enrollment), the patient remains on treatment with stable disease. Kaplan-Meier curves for EFS and OS are shown in Supplementary Fig. S2. Survival summaries are provided in Fig. 2B.

sec.title: Biomarker analysis
sec.p: Of the 17 patients, 10 (58.8%) had PD-L1 CPS ≥5, 9 (52.9%) in CPS ≥ 10, and 8 (47.1%) in CPS ≥ 20. The mean CPS was 19.2. The relationship between PD-L1 CPS and TRG is summarized in Supplementary Table S2. An exploratory analysis suggested a numerical trend towards a higher MPR rate in patients with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 20 (57.1%, 4/7, 95%CI: 0.18–0.90) compared to those with CPS < 20 (22.2%, 2/9, 95%CI: 0.03–0.60).

To explore potential biomarkers of response to neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy in EBVaGC, dynamic changes in tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) were evaluated using multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) on paired pre- and post-neoadjuvant therapy biopsy specimens from 11 patients. Among these patients, five patients (patients 1, 2, 3, 6, and 15) achieved MPR, but not in six patients (patients 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, and 13) (Fig. 3A). Pre-neoadjuvant therapy TIME was compared between MPR and non-MPR groups. CD8+ T cell infiltration was significantly higher in the MPR group (p = 0.032), particularly in the tumor parenchyma (p = 0.032), but not in the stromal region (p = 0.126) (Fig. 3B). M1 macrophage (CD68+CD163−) infiltration was also significantly higher in non-MPR stromal regions (p = 0.03), whereas M2 macrophages (CD68+CD163+) did not differ significantly (p = 0.931).Fig. 3Analysis of tumor immune microenvironment related to neoadjuvant therapy efficacy.

Paired specimens (n = 10) were analyzed to evaluate changes in TIME before and after neoadjuvant therapy, with analyses focused on the stromal compartment due to loss of tumor parenchyma following treatment. A significant post-neoadjuvant therapy reduction in M1 macrophage density was observed (p = 0.049). Within-group comparisons in MPR and non-MPR patients showed no statistically significant difference in immune cell shifts. At the individual level, 83% (5/6) of non-MPR patients showed a decrease in M1 macrophages post-neoadjuvant therapy, versus 50% (2/4) in the MPR group. Conversely, 83% (5/6) of non-MPR patients had increased CD8+ T cells post-neoadjuvant therapy, compared with only 25% (1/4) in the MPR group (Fig. 3C). Four non-MPR patients (patients 5, 7, 10, and 13) showed a pattern of increased CD8+ T cells with decreased M1 macrophages; one MPR patient (patient 3) showed the opposite. (Source data 2, source data are provided as a Source Data file)

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study is the first prospective clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of perioperative immunochemotherapy in patients with locally advanced EBVaGC. A total of 17 patients with locally advanced, resectable disease (clinical stage cT3/4aNxM0 or cT2N + M0) were enrolled. The perioperative immunochemotherapy demonstrated favorable pathological responses, including an MPR rate of 37.5% (95%CI: 0.15–0.65), a pCR rate of 25% (95%CI: 0.07–0.52), and an R0 resection rate of 100% (95%CI: 0.79–1.00), with 81.3% (95%CI: 0.54–0.96) of patients achieving ypN0. The regimen was well tolerated overall, with grade 3–4 TRAEs observed in only 35.3% of patients. After a median follow-up of 29.8 months (95% CI: 26.2 months-41.8 months), only 2 patients experienced disease recurrence, and 1 death was recorded.

Patients with EBVaGC demonstrated a moderate pathological response to neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. The MPR rate in our cohort compares favorably with the 26.8% (127/474) recently reported in the MATTERHORN trial. The pCR rate (25.0%, ypT0N0) was higher than that reported in non–molecularly stratified cohorts with locally advanced gastric cancer: 12.9% (ypT0N0, 52/402) in the KEYNOTE-585 trial4, 18.3% (ypT0, 33/180) in the DRAGON IV trial28, 19.2% (ypT0N0, 91/474) in the MATTERHORN trial5, and 22.2% (ypT0N0, 12/54) in the NEOSUMMIT-01 trial7. In addition, the ypT0 rate in our cohort was 31.3% (95%CI: 0.11–0.59), slightly higher than the 25.0% (2/8) ypT0 rate observed in the EBVaGC subgroup of the DRAGON IV trial. Nevertheless, the pCR rate observed in our study remains lower than those reported in certain molecular subtypes of gastric cancer, such as MSI-H and HER2-positive subtypes9–11. The MPR rate in our cohort was lower than that reported in unselected populations treated with neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy: 44.4% (24/54) in NEOSUMMIT-017, 51.1% (92/180) in DRAGON IV28, and 63.3% (19/30) in a phase II trial29.

Patients with EBVaGC presented with a higher burden of nodal disease at baseline but exhibited substantial nodal downstaging following neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. All patients had cN+ at baseline. 64.7% (11/17) of EBVaGC patients had baseline cN2-3, a proportion notably higher than that reported in other perioperative immunochemotherapy trials for locally advanced gastric cancer, including 36.3% (146/402) in KEYNOTE-5854, 48.9% (88/180) in DRAGON IV28, and 55.6% (30/54) in NEOSUMMIT-017. Despite the heavier nodal burden at baseline, 81.3% (13/16, 95%CI: 0.54–0.96) of surgical patients achieved ypN0 status, surpassing corresponding rates observed in MATTERHORN (55.9%, 241/431), DRAGON IV (46.1%, 83/180), NEOSUMMIT-01 (40.7%, 22/54), and DANTE (67.8%, 99/146)30. Given that lymph node metastasis is a well-established independent predictor of postoperative recurrence in gastric cancer31,32, the observed reduction in nodal disease burden through neoadjuvant immunotherapy may translate into a lower risk of recurrence and improved long-term outcomes in EBVaGC patients treated with perioperative immunochemotherapy.

High PD-L1 expression is a hallmark of EBVaGC15,33. The underlying mechanisms are multifaceted, involving both viral protein and miRNA-mediated regulation. Beyond the established role of LMP1 in activating PD-L1 transcription through the NF-κB pathway34,35, recent studies reveal that EBV-encoded miRNAs, particularly BART11 and BART17-3p, directly promote PD-L1 upregulation by targeting the transcriptional repressors FOXP1 and PBRM136. Concurrently, EBV fosters an inflamed yet suppressed tumor microenvironment. Single-cell analyses have identified a pivotal antigen-specific ISG-15+CD8+ T-cell population that is highly enriched in EBVaGC and represents a transitory exhaustion state; the reinvigoration of this population upon immunochemotherapy critically determines treatment response37. Our clinical findings align with this multifaceted biology. The observed numerical trend towards a higher MPR rate in patients with elevated PD-L1 CPS reflects the cumulative effect of these viral mechanisms. More importantly, the significantly higher baseline density of CD8⁺ T cells in the MPR group provides cellular evidence for the pre-existing, EBV-imprinted T-cell response described in single-cell studies. While the predictive value of individual biomarkers in our small cohort requires further validation, these results collectively underscore EBVaGC as a compelling model for connecting viral oncogenesis to exploitable cancer immunity.

At a median follow-up of 29.8 months (95% CI: 26.2 months-41.8 months), the median OS had not yet been reached. The early survival curves exhibited a plateau, suggesting a potential for durable long-term survival. This favorable outcome may be attributed to enhanced sensitivity to immune-based therapy in EBVaGC and the specific treatment strategy employed. The selection of the doublet chemotherapy backbone aligns with established regional standards and high-level evidence from Asian populations38,39, while the four-cycle neoadjuvant duration was designed to maximize immune activation4, a rationale underscored by trials suggesting the limited efficacy of adjuvant-only immunotherapy40. This is supported by the deep pathological responses observed in most patients, including a high rate of ypN0, as well as the enrichment of MPR among those with high PD-L1 CPS. Besides, this study indicated that the combination of toripalimab and CapeOX is associated with a favorable safety profile, with no grade 5 TRAEs reported. Furthermore, treatment adherence and perioperative feasibility were high. All enrolled patients completed neoadjuvant toripalimab plus CapeOX (100% vs 94.5% in MATTERHORN), and 94.1% (16/17) proceeded to surgery. Among surgical patients, 93.8% (15/16) initiated adjuvant therapy and 62.5% (10/16) completed all planned adjuvant cycles (vs 87.4% and 55.6% in MATTERHORN). Surgical timing was largely preserved: 81.3% underwent surgery as scheduled; postponement occurred in 18.7% (3/16), comparable to MATTERHORN (11.7%).

The TIME plays a pivotal role in regulating immune surveillance and immune evasion41. To further elucidate the mechanistic role of TIME in treatment response or resistance, this study employed mIF in paired pre- and post-neoadjuvant therapy tumor specimens. The analysis revealed that the baseline proportion of CD8⁺ T cells was significantly higher in the MPR group compared to the non-MPR group, with this difference primarily localized to the tumor parenchyma. This suggests that CD8⁺ T cells within the parenchyma may play a critical role in mediating pathological response. This observation is consistent with prior studies identifying CD8⁺ T cell infiltration as a favorable predictor of response to immunotherapy42,43. In the analysis of dynamic changes in CD8⁺ T cells and M1 macrophages before and after neoadjuvant therapy, we observed an intriguing trend: most non-MPR patients exhibited an increase in stromal CD8⁺ T cell infiltration post-neoadjuvant therapy, whereas the majority of MPR patients showed a decrease in CD8⁺ T cell density. It is critical to note that this finding is derived from a limited sample size and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. One plausible explanation for the relative decrease in CD8+ T cells among MPR patients is the extensive tumor cell elimination leading to a reduced tumor antigen burden and a consequent contraction of the number of antigen-specific T cells. In contrast, the persistent tumor antigen burden in non-MPR patients might drive continued T cell recruitment and proliferation. Furthermore, the robust T cell response in MPR patients might lead to T cell exhaustion or the activation of negative feedback mechanisms, resulting in their subsequent decline. This trend did not appear to correlate with changes in M1 macrophage levels, which generally declined in the stroma of most patients post-treatment. These preliminary findings suggest that, compared with M1 macrophages, CD8⁺ T cells may serve as a more sensitive and potentially more predictive biomarker for assessing response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in EBVaGC. Future studies with larger cohorts are imperative to validate this observation.

As an exploratory study, several important limitations should be noted. First, no formal sample size calculation was performed, as the primary goal was to obtain preliminary results of efficacy and safety; consequently, the findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger, statistically powered trials. Second, as an exploratory, single-arm trial without a concurrent control group, it is unable to delineate the specific contribution of toripalimab from that of chemotherapy, and the findings should be interpreted with caution. Third, the relatively small sample size, while reflective of the challenge in recruiting this specific molecular subtype, limits the strength of our conclusions. Finally, as all participants were enrolled from a Chinese population, the generalizability of our findings to other ethnic groups remains uncertain. Nonetheless, we sought to strengthen the study through rigorous clinical staging, including diagnostic laparoscopy, and by incorporating exploratory biomarker analyses to generate robust hypotheses for future research.

In conclusion, this prospective study represents the first completed clinical trial to report on the efficacy and safety of perioperative toripalimab plus CapeOX in patients with locally advanced EBVaGC. Exploratory analyses suggest that PD-L1 expression and CD8⁺ T cell infiltration may correlate with treatment response, highlighting potential predictive biomarkers.

sec.title: Ethics statement
sec.p: The study protocol (The full study protocol is provided in the Supplementary Information file) was approved by the Ethics Committee of Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (NCT04744649). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to study enrollment. This trial was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines44.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: The NICE study (NCT04744649) is a multicenter, open-label, phase II clinical trial conducted in China, designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of perioperative toripalimab combined with CapeOX in patients with locally advanced, resectable GC/GEJC. Patients were stratified by biomarker status into three cohorts: PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) ≥5 (assessed by IHC 22C3; cohort A), EBV-associated (cohort B), and mismatch repair deficiency/microsatellite instability–high (deficient mismatch repair/microsatellite instability-high; cohort C). The current report focuses on cohort B, which was an exploratory, single-arm study without a formal statistical power calculation. The primary goal was to obtain preliminary estimates of efficacy and safety for this novel combination in a defined population, generating hypotheses for future studies. Eligible patients were required to have histologically or cytologically confirmed GC/GEJC with clinical staging of cT3/4aNxM0 or cT2N + M0, based on the AJCC 8th edition. Staging evaluation included CT or MRI, diagnostic laparoscopy, and peritoneal cytology. EBV positivity was confirmed by in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNAs (EBER). Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are provided in the study protocol. Patients were enrolled between May 12, 2021, and September 21, 2023. The final follow-up was conducted on January 31, 2025.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: All patients received 4 cycles of neoadjuvant therapy consisting of toripalimab in combination with the CapeOX regimen. Toripalimab was administered at a fixed dose of 240 mg via intravenous infusion on day 1 of each 3-week cycle. The CapeOX regimen included oxaliplatin 130 mg/m² intravenously on day 1 and capecitabine 1000 mg/m²orally twice daily on days 1–14 of each 3-week cycle. Surgery was performed four-six weeks after the completion of neoadjuvant therapy. Six weeks postoperatively, patients began receiving adjuvant treatment, with the same neoadjuvant regimen.

Baseline and preoperative tumor staging for patients was determined by contrast-enhanced abdominal CT, diagnostic laparoscopy, and peritoneal lavage cytology. Safety monitoring was conducted in accordance with the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI-CTCAE) version 4.03. Surgical complications were classified according to the Clavien-Dindo grading system45. Pathological responses of the primary tumor and regional lymph nodes after neoadjuvant therapy were assessed according to the Tumor Regression Grading (TRG) criteria46,47. MPR was defined as ≤ 10% residual viable tumor cells in the resected specimen upon microscopic examination. All enrolled patients underwent biomarker testing and hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining for pathological evaluation. All pathological assessments were independently reviewed by two blinded gastrointestinal pathologists at the central laboratory (Nanfang Hospital), with any discrepancies resolved by consensus discussion.

sec.title: Study endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the MPR rate (proportion of patients achieving MPR in the resected primary tumor). The secondary endpoints included: (1) pCR rate, defined as the absence of residual tumor cells in both the primary tumor and lymph nodes after neoadjuvant therapy; (2) R0 resection rate, defined as the proportion of patients achieving microscopically margin-negative resection; (3) Incidence of adverse events, defined as any treatment-related adverse events occurring during therapy and up to 3 months post-treatment; (4) Event-free survival (EFS), defined as the time from enrollment to the occurrence of any of the following events: disease progression, recurrence, or death from any cause, whichever occurred first; (5) Overall survival (OS), defined as the time from enrollment to death from any cause; (6) Tumor microenvironment, tissues were assessed by multiplex immunofluorescence. All endpoints were prespecified in the study protocol

sec.title: In situ hybridization for EBER
sec.p: EBV detection was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) gastric cancer tissue samples using in situ hybridization (ISH) with an EBER probe kit (ZSGB-BIO, catalog no. ISH-7001). Tissue sections were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through graded ethanol (100%, 95%, and 75%). Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked by incubation with blocking solution for 10 min at room temperature in the dark, followed by rinsing in distilled water and rehydration through an ethanol gradient (75%, 95%, and 100%, 2 min each). Subsequently, tissue sections were digested with pepsin working solution at 37 °C for 30 minutes, followed again by ethanol dehydration. Approximately 10–20 μL of digoxigenin-labeled EBER probe was applied to each section, which was then covered with a coverslip and sealed with rubber cement. Hybridization was carried out at 37 °C for 2 h in a humidified chamber. Following hybridization, rubber cement was removed, and slides were immersed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 10 min to allow coverslips to detach. Slides were washed three times in PBS (2 min each), then incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)–conjugated anti-digoxigenin antibody at 30 °C for 30 min. After three additional PBS washes, slides were incubated with freshly prepared 3,3’-diaminobenzidine (DAB) substrate at room temperature for 5–10 min for signal development. Slides were rinsed with tap water and counterstained with hematoxylin for 5–10 s, followed by differentiation and bluing to enhance nuclear contrast.

sec.title: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining
sec.p: IHC was performed on 4-μm-thick tissue sections using an automated IHC stainer (Ventana, Tucson, AZ, USA). The assessment of PD-L1 protein expression in GC is a qualitative immunohistochemical assay that uses anti-PD-L1 antibodies(Dako, 22C3, 1:200) to detect PD-L1 protein in FFPE tissues from gastric adenocarcinomas. A minimum of 100 tumor cells must be present in the PD-L1-stained slide for the specimen to be considered adequate for PD-L1 evaluation. CPS is the total number of positively stained PD-L1 cells (i.e., tumor cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages) divided by the total number of viable tumor cells, multiplied by 100%. MMR status was assessed by IHC using monoclonal antibodies for anti-mutL homolog 1 (MLH1, Abnova, H00004292-M02, 1:100), anti-mutS homolog 2 (MSH2, BD Bioscience, G219-1129, 1:100), anti-postmeiotic segregation increased 2 (PMS2, BD Bioscience, A16-4, 1:100), and anti-mutS homolog 6 (MSH6, Abcam, ab99889, 1:100). Tumors lacking either MLH1, MSH2, PMS2, or MSH6 expression were considered MMR deficient (dMMR), whereas tumors that maintained expression of MLH1, MSH2, PMS2, and MSH6 were considered MMR proficient (pMMR). HER2 expression, which was monitoring of IHC stains using monoclonal antibodies (Ventana, 4B5, 1:100), was graded using a score scale of 0 to 3.

sec.title: TIME by multiplex immunofluorescence mIF
sec.p: Multiplex immunofluorescence staining was conducted using the Akoya OPAL Polaris 7-Color Automation IHC kit (NEL871001KT). FFPE tissue slides were first deparaffinized in a BOND RX system (Leica Biosystems) and then incubated sequentially with primary antibodies targeting CD163 (Abcam, ab182422, 1:500), CD68 (Abcam, ab213363, 1:1000), PD-1 (CST, D4W2J, 86163S, 1:200), PD-L1 (CST, E1L3N, 13684S, 1:400), CD3 (Dako, A0452 IR503, 1:1), CD4 (Abcam, ab133616, 1:100), CD8 (Abcam, ab178089, 1:200), CD56 (Abcam, ab75813, 1:1000), CD20 (Dako, L26 IR604, 1:1), FOXP3 (Abcam, ab20034, 1:100) and pan-CK (Abcam, ab7753, 1:100) (Akoya Biosciences). Notably, a subset of samples was only assessed for PD-L1, CD8, CD56, CD68, CD163, and pan-CK. This was followed by incubation with secondary antibodies and corresponding reactive Opal fluorophores. Nucleic acids were stained with DAPI. Tissue slides that were bound with primary and secondary antibodies but not fluorophores were included as negative controls to assess autofluorescence. Multiplex-stained slides were scanned using a Vectra Polaris Quantitative Pathology Imaging System(Akoya Biosciences) at 20 nm wavelength intervals from 440 nm to 780 nm with a fixed exposure time and an absolute magnification of × 200. All scans for each slide were then superimposed to obtain a single image. Fluorescence images were imported and analyzed using the AP-TIME software developed by 3D Medicines. Tumor parenchyma and stroma were differentiated by Pan-CK staining. The quantities of various cell populations were expressed as the number of stained cells per square millimeter and as the percentage of positively stained cells in all nucleated cells.

For image analysis, regions of interest (ROIs) were meticulously delineated by a certified pathologist to ensure representativeness. The selection prioritized tumor regions with well-preserved morphology, robust staining quality, and maximal tumor content, while explicitly excluding areas of non-tumor tissue. Cell quantification was performed using the AP-TIME software, with positive cells identified based on a predefined staining intensity threshold. All cell counts within each ROI were performed by two independent observers, and any discrepancies were resolved through consensus discussion. The average number of positive cells per ROI was used for subsequent analysis.

sec.title: Pathological response assessment
sec.p: Pathological response was assessed for all 16 patients who underwent surgery. The assessment of pathological response, including MPR and pCR, was conducted according to the following standardized procedure to ensure objectivity and consistency: All resected primary tumor specimens were comprehensively evaluated with standard hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The entire tumor bed was examined to identify and quantify the percentage of residual viable tumor cells. All pathological assessments were performed by two independent, blinded pathologists at the central laboratory (Nanfang Hospital). The inter-observer concordance for the quantification of residual tumor percentage between the two pathologists was excellent, with an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.965 (P < 0.001). In cases where the two pathologists had discrepant findings regarding the quantification of residual tumor, a consensus-based approach was employed. This involved a joint re-review of the H&E slides to reach a final diagnosis. If a consensus could not be reached, a third senior pathologist would be enlisted for arbitration (although this was not required in the current study cohort).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: This was a single-arm, exploratory trial with a non-randomized design. No blinding was applied to investigators or study staff during treatment assignment. Continuous variables were reported as medians (range), and categorical variables as counts (percentages). Kaplan–Meier methodology was used to estimate EFS and OS. Median follow-up time and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method. For comparisons of immune cell proportions between independent groups, a two-sided Mann–Whitney U test was used. No multiple-comparison adjustment was applied unless otherwise specified. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 28.0) and R software (version 4.4.0).
